turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response: Well, doc, my family brought me in. See, I was at the county fair... I've been going to that fair since I was a boy, back when my daddy used to show his prize-winning Angus. He had this one bull, Big Jim, meanest thing you ever saw, but he won a blue ribbon in '78. Anyway, I was giving a talk at the fair, and... I just had to show them. I climbed right up onto the tractor, right in the middle of it all. I kept jerking the controls, you know, back and forth, trying to show the crowd the 'new pattern.' It made so much sense in my head. People started yelling at me to get down, but... I couldn't make myself stop. It was like I had to finish showing them. The tractors they make nowadays, though, they don't have the same weight to 'em. Not like the old John Deeres. You ever drive one of those?

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, wandering off-topic to discuss his father's prize-winning bull and the weight of old tractors.
symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient describes engaging in highly inappropriate and uncontrollable behavior by climbing onto a tractor during a talk and jerking the controls despite people yelling at him to stop.

turns.doctor_question: Before this incident at the fair, have you ever had other times in your life when you felt unusually energetic, needed very little sleep, or had racing thoughts that lasted for days or weeks?
turns.patient_response: Well, energy... yeah, I suppose. Lately, most nights I don't even bother going to bed. I just sit in my old recliner, maybe sleep two or three hours, or not at all. But then I'm up before the sun, feeling completely charged, ready to work the whole place like nothing happened. You know, that recliner... I bought it at a yard sale out on Route 9, must have been fifteen years ago. Old Mrs. Higgins was selling off her husband's things after he passed. He was a good man, Arthur Higgins. Grew the best sweet corn in the county. We used to trade a quarter of beef for a truckload of his corn every August. The secret, he always said, was the soil... you gotta have the right mix of nitrogen. Anyway, yeah, I just don't seem to need much rest lately.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, wandering off-topic to discuss a yard sale, a neighbor, and sweet corn before returning to the subject of sleep.
symptom_reasoning.S034: The patient confirms having unusual energy, describing feeling 'completely charged' and ready to work despite lack of sleep.
symptom_reasoning.S036: The patient explicitly states they sleep only two or three hours or not at all, yet wake up feeling fully rested and energized.

turns.doctor_question: Before this recent period where you've been sleeping very little and feeling energized, have you ever had other times in your life—maybe months or years ago—when you felt similarly high-energy and didn't need much sleep for several days in a row?
turns.patient_response:
Other times? Well, I can't say that I have. No, I don't think so. Usually, running a place like mine just wears a man down, plain and simple. Especially in the spring. You take calving season, for instance. Now, back in '94, we had a late blizzard right in the middle of it. Wind came howling down from Canada like a freight train. I was out in the snow for... gosh, must have been three days straight, pulling calves. 

Had this one first-calf heifer get herself stuck down by the lower creek bed. I had to hook up the winch on the old Ford just to drag her out of the muck before she froze to death. That truck was a beauty, though. A '79 F-150, two-tone, blue and white. My boy finally blew the transmission on it a few years back, but it had over three hundred thousand miles on it by then. You just can't kill one of those old inline-six engines. They run forever if you keep the oil clean. 

But anyway... what was it you asked? Oh, feeling energized. No, I don't remember feeling like this before. Usually I'm just bone tired and trying to keep my eyes open.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, drifting from the original question about past energy levels into a long, unrelated story about calving season, a blizzard, and an old truck before finally returning to the question.

top_partial.disease_name: Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features

turns.doctor_question: Before this recent period at the fair and all this energy you've been having, did you ever notice any strange experiences—like hearing voices, seeing things others didn't see, or feeling like people were trying to harm you or send you special messages?
turns.patient_response:
Well, strange experiences... yeah, I suppose so. Even before all this energy hit me, before the fair and all that... there were a few weeks where things were pretty quiet. I wasn't feeling all revved up or anything, just doing my chores. But I kept hearing the power lines talking. You know, out by the county road, where the lines run from the main grid down to my property. They put those up back in... oh, must have been the late '80s. The electric company sent this crew down from the city, didn't know a thing about respecting a man's fence lines. Left a gate open and three of my best yearlings got out onto the highway. Took me half the day to round 'em up. 

But anyway, yeah, during those quiet weeks, I'd be out there and I could hear the lines talking to me. And the farm data, too. I get these reports, you know, crop yields, soil moisture, all that from the ag extension office. They send 'em in these thick manila envelopes. My granddad used to keep all his records in ledgers. Beautiful handwriting he had, all cursive, written with a fountain pen. You don't see handwriting like that anymore. They don't teach it in schools. Now it's all computers and typing. 

But I'd look at that farm data they sent me, and I just knew... I believed it was carrying hidden warnings. Like someone was trying to tell me something through the numbers. Even when I wasn't feeling all full of energy, I still heard the lines and I still saw those warnings in the data.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient describes a fixed belief that farm data reports were carrying hidden warnings and messages.
symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient reports experiencing auditory hallucinations, specifically hearing power lines talking to him.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, going off on unrelated tangents about an electric company crew in the 1980s and his grandfather's cursive handwriting.

turns.doctor_question: When you were hearing those voices in the power lines and seeing the hidden warnings in the farm data during those quiet weeks you mentioned—before you started feeling all this energy—how were you feeling mood-wise? Were you feeling sad, depressed, or down at all during that time, or did you feel pretty normal?
turns.patient_response:
Mood-wise? No, I wasn't sad or depressed or anything like that. I felt fine, really. Like I was saying, there were several of those quieter weeks when I was not especially energized or feeling grand, you know? Just going about my regular chores, not feeling too high or too low. But even without all that extra energy, I still heard the lines talking, and I still believed the farm data was carrying those hidden warnings. 

The data... you know, that reminds me, the soil test that month showed we were real low on phosphorus. Phosphorus is a funny thing. It doesn't wash out of the soil like nitrogen does, it just binds up and sits there. My neighbor, Bill Jenkins, he tried fixing his phosphorus problem one year by spreading turkey litter all over his north forty. Lord, the smell of that stuff. We had a stiff south wind for three days straight, and my wife—she passed about ten years ago now—she flat out refused to open a single window in the house. She had these beautiful lace curtains she ordered from the J.C. Penney catalog... must have been 1985. Took six weeks to ship all the way out here, and she didn't want the turkey dust getting into the lace. She was always particular about keeping the dust out, which is a full-time job on a dirt road. 

But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, yeah. No, I wasn't feeling down at all during those weeks. Just a normal, quiet mood, even with the lines talking to me.

symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient confirms experiencing auditory hallucinations, stating he 'heard the lines talking'.

turns.doctor_question: You mentioned hearing the power lines talk and seeing warnings in the farm data during those quiet weeks when you were feeling normal. Are you still hearing those voices in the power lines and seeing those hidden messages in the farm data right now, today?
turns.patient_response:
Right now? Today? Well, yes, I suppose I am. Matter of fact, during the months when I was sleeping hardly at all and pushing the farm expansion day and night, I was also hearing voices in the irrigation lines and reading warnings in the yield maps. 

We put in a whole new center pivot system for that expansion. Cost an absolute fortune, all that galvanized steel. Used to be we just ran wheel lines, or handlines before that. You ever have to move aluminum handlines in the dark? It's a miserable job. The mud gets so thick it'll suck the boots right off your feet. My youngest, Tommy, he lost a brand new pair of Red Wing boots out in the east pasture doing that back in... oh, must have been '04. Just stepped in a boggy patch and the mud kept the boots. He had to walk a mile back to the house in his socks. We laughed about it later, but those boots weren't cheap. Red Wings used to be the best you could buy, stitched right here in America. Now you check the tags and half of them are made overseas. 

It’s a crying shame what’s happening to manufacturing in this country. Just like the tractors... everything is computerized now. You can't even fix your own engine without plugging it into a laptop. The combine spits out those yield maps with the GPS, all these red and green grids showing the moisture and bushels per acre. You almost need a computer degree just to harvest corn these days. But I could see the warnings right there in the grids on the maps, clear as day, just like the voices in the pipes. So, yeah, they're still there today.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient confirms seeing hidden warnings in the farm yield maps, indicating referential delusions.
symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient confirms hearing voices in the irrigation lines and pipes, indicating auditory hallucinations.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, wandering into a long, loosely related story about irrigation systems, lost boots, and manufacturing before returning to the topic.
symptom_reasoning.S036: The patient mentions a period of 'sleeping hardly at all,' indicating a decreased need for sleep.
symptom_reasoning.S040: The patient describes 'pushing the farm expansion day and night,' demonstrating increased goal-directed activity.

turns.doctor_question: When did you first start hearing those voices in the power lines and seeing the hidden warnings in the farm data? Was that happening months or years ago, or did it all start around the same time you began sleeping very little and feeling all that energy at the fair?
turns.patient_response:
When did it start? Well, let me think... the voices and those coded warnings, they've been happening for about 11 months now. Yeah, right around 11 months. 

That would put it back to late last summer. We were just getting ready for the county fair, actually, but not this year's fair, the one before. The county fair is a big deal around here. My daughter-in-law, Sarah, she enters her preserves every year. She makes this jalapeño peach jam that'll knock your socks off. Sweet at first, and then it just bites you right in the back of the throat. She won a blue ribbon for it three years running. Course, the judging is always a little political. Old Mrs. Higgins has been on the judging committee since the Carter administration, and she always favors the traditional strawberry or blackberry. Thinks anything with a pepper in it belongs in a salsa jar, not on a biscuit. 

But Sarah, she just smiles and keeps entering it. She's a good girl, Sarah. Met my boy at the state agricultural college. They had a beautiful wedding out by the old oak tree on the south pasture. We strung up lights all through the branches... took me three days on the cherry picker to get 'em all hung right. Had to rent a generator just to run 'em because the extension cords wouldn't reach that far from the barn. 

But anyway, yeah, it's been about 11 months since all that started with the lines and the warnings. Long before I started feeling all that energy and running on no sleep.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient confirms experiencing 'coded warnings' (delusions) for about 11 months.
symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient confirms hearing 'voices' (hallucinations) for about 11 months.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, wandering into a long, unrelated story about jam and a wedding before returning to the original topic.
symptom_reasoning.S034: The patient mentions a distinct period of 'feeling all that energy'.
symptom_reasoning.S036: The patient mentions a distinct period of 'running on no sleep'.

turns.doctor_question: So if the voices and the hidden warnings in the farm data started about 11 months ago, and then the high energy and barely sleeping started more recently—can you tell me roughly when the high energy and the sleeping very little began? Was that weeks ago, or months ago?
turns.patient_response:
Well, let me figure that out. The energy, the not needing any sleep... that's been going on for a long time now. I'd say those charged up, sleepless, nonstop stretches have taken up about 10 months of this past year or so. 

It's funny how time just slips away when you're moving that fast. Reminds me of the year we decided to completely overhaul the combine harvester ourselves. Must have been late November, right after we got the last of the soybeans out. Soybeans are tricky, you know. You gotta catch 'em when the moisture is just right, otherwise they shatter in the pods and you leave half your profit laying right there on the dirt. My daddy used to say farming soybeans was like trying to catch rain in a sieve. 

Anyway, we pulled that combine into the main shop. It's a big Morton building, insulated, got a concrete floor we poured ourselves back in '92. Took five cement trucks to pour that floor. The driver of the third truck, a fella named Earl, he backed up too far and took out the gutter on the side of the barn. Bent it right in half. We had to order a custom piece from a sheet metal place two towns over just to match the profile. They don't make that specific gutter shape anymore, you see. Everything now is seamless aluminum, rolled right off a truck in your driveway. 

But yeah, we had that combine torn down to the bare frame all winter long. Parts everywhere. So, to answer your question, those high energy, sleepless times have been going on for about 10 months out of the last year.
